div.p: A life update of Barbara Hepworth to Leonard Woolf, in which she describes her current work and living situation, as well as her recent exhibition of paintings. She also reminisces about the past and expresses her gratitude for the support she received from Woolf during the war.

I don't know if you can still be at Monk's House,
but I feel I must write to you to say what a pleasure
it was to hear your voice again, in the broadcast on
Mecklenburgh Square. I do hope all is going well with you?
I enjoyed the programme very much, it brought up such
nostalgic pictures of days that now seem a very long time
ago.
I'm afraid I have rather lost touch with most of my
friends in the publishing world. Life grows ever more
busy for me, as for everyone else, or increasingly difficult
to see people no longer directly in one's path. I am now
completely in art teaching, dividing my time between
physically handicapped children in a London Special
School and adults in a College at Barnet. I like it
very much. Margaret is in the same thing, she teaches
in a secretarial College at Kensington, sending young
girls out to 16-17 a week jobs - it's incredible to
think that twenty years ago we were advertising
posts for juniors at 15/- and getting hundreds of
applicants! So we both have the long holidays which
we greatly appreciate which give us the chance of
some trips of our own.
I had an exhibition of my paintings in a local
pub. This spring which was successful beyond my
wildest hopes: I had a good press in a modest way,
and sold 18 pictures, which created quite a sensation
in the neighbourhood! Do you remember giving me the
introduction to Duncan Grant just after the war when I
had made up my mind to study painting? He suggested
Camberwell, and it was an exceptionally lucky moment
to go there, when Coldstream & PassmorePasmore & Rogers were
running the painting school. Much later, Lawrence Gowing,
whom I also met there, & Julia Strachey offered me a
very tempting appointment at Kings College, Newcastle,
but it was chiefly on the administration side of things
again, and, after some near-searching, I turned it down.
I haven't regretted it; I like teaching & I have more
time for my own work — but it is free lance & precarious,
& I suppose it won't be much longer before I feel
the lack of security & pension at the end that
I've turned away from!
Hearing about Mecklenburgh Square again made me
wish it were still possible to find somewhere to live in
Bloomsbury, some tucked-away square away from
the traffic & noise. We are among the people who
are turned out under the rent act in October, with
a 'bad landlord' who won't negotiate. Having failed
to find anywhere else to go that we can afford, we
shall have to outstay our welcome under the new
amendment: I hope not for too long & that it
won't be too unpleasant a business.
Margaret sends her best regards to you —
remembers the time when you took us in as
refugees & made us welcome at Monks HouseMonk's House in
those queer confused days at the beginning of
the war.
div.closer:
with warm good wishes & remembrances, yours ever
Barbara
